title: Sprouted Seeds Inside Squash: What It Means and Whether You Can Eat It

seo.title: Sprouted Seeds Inside Squash: Is It Safe to Eat?
seo.meta_description: Seeds can germinate inside an older squash, a phenomenon called vivipary. Sprouting does not make the flesh toxic by itself; if the squash is firm, clean-smelling, and free of rot or mold, the flesh can be cooked.
seo.search_intent: Explain vivipary in winter squash and whether sprouted seeds affect safety, flavor, or quality.

excerpt: Sprouted seeds inside squash are a maturity phenomenon called vivipary, not automatic spoilage. If the flesh is firm and normal-smelling with no mold, wet rot, or extreme bitterness, it can still be eaten.
content_html:
Cut open a stored spaghetti squash or pumpkin and you may find something that looks impossible: white roots and shoots growing from the seed cavity. The seeds have begun to germinate while still inside the fruit, a process called vivipary.

It is unusual in the kitchen but not mysterious. Seed dormancy can break as a squash ages and storage conditions line up for germination.

Does sprouting make the squash unsafe?

No, not by itself. University extension experts have specifically addressed sprouting pumpkin and squash seeds and consider the flesh usable when the fruit itself is sound.

The bigger issue is quality. A squash old enough for internal sprouting may be drier, stringier, less sweet, or otherwise past its best.

Inspect the flesh separately

Firm flesh with a normal color and smell is reassuring. Water-soaked rot, slime, fuzzy mold, leaking tissue, or a fermented odor are spoilage signs and should drive the decision regardless of the sprouts.

Also stop if the squash tastes intensely and unusually bitter. Extreme bitterness in cucurbit-family produce is a separate warning sign and is not explained by harmless vivipary.

Do you have to eat the sprouts?

No. Scoop out the entire seed cavity, sprouts included, just as you normally remove seeds before roasting many winter squashes. Sprouted seeds are not automatically hazardous, but their texture is not necessarily good for roasting.

Why it often happens late in storage

Winter squash can keep for months under good conditions. Over time, seed dormancy weakens. Temperature, moisture, genetics, and fruit maturity all influence whether a seed decides to grow before the fruit is opened.

Sprouts are not worms and they did not enter through the rind

Vivipary starts with seeds that were already inside the fruit. A completely intact squash can therefore contain surprisingly long white shoots. That is why the finding can look alarming without indicating an insect infestation.

If you are deciding whether a white structure is a sprout or mold, trace it to the seed. A sprouting root emerges from an individual seed with an organized shape. Mold tends to grow as fuzzy or film-like colonies over surrounding tissue and often appears with decay.

Vivipary is not a safety certificate for the whole fruit

The fact that internal sprouting is a normal plant phenomenon does not guarantee that every other part of the squash is sound. A squash can have germinated seeds and an unrelated rotten area at the same time. Evaluate the sprouts as one observation and the flesh as another. That separation prevents both unnecessary waste and an overly casual response to genuine decay.

Bottom line

A white sprout is not the same thing as white mold. If the squash flesh is firm, sound, and normal-tasting, remove the seed cavity and cook it. If the fruit has genuine rot, discard it for the rot—not because a seed germinated.

faq.question: What are the white sprouts inside my squash?
faq.answer: They are seeds that germinated inside the fruit, a phenomenon called vivipary.

faq.question: Does vivipary make squash poisonous?
faq.answer: No. Sprouting itself does not make sound squash flesh toxic. Judge the flesh for rot, mold, off odors, and abnormal bitterness.

faq.question: Can I scoop out the sprouted seeds and cook the squash?
faq.answer: Yes, if the flesh is firm and sound. Remove the seed cavity as you normally would and cook the remaining flesh.
